newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi army accused of forcing Hutus into camps.
newsitem.headline: Burundi army accused of forcing Hutus into camps.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International on Tuesday accused Burundi's mainly Tutsi army of forcing majority Hutus into camps, leading to massacres of hundreds of them.
The London-based group said Burundian military authorities forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to leave their homes and live in camps, creating a new category of displaced people.

"This regroupment policy applies almost exclusively to the Hutu ethnic group, which is effectively trapped in appalling and life-threatening conditions in the camps or which becomes a military target outside the camps," an Amnesty report said.
A military junta led by retired army major Pierre Buyoya says the "regroupment camps" are for the protection of the inhabitants and that regroupment applies to all ethnic groups equally.
Burundi's Tutsi army is at war with Hutu rebels.
But Amnesty International said it had received numerous testimonies which showed that, in the majority of cases, the local Hutu population had been moved into the camps by force.
"A pattern of mass human rights violations committed during or after the process of regroupment undermines any argument that this regroupment provides protection," Amnesty added.
Amnesty said estimates of people confined in regroupment camps varied from 350,000 to 500,000 people.
The global human rights watchdog spoke of "killings, house destruction, looting and rape", during regroupment operations.
"During regroupment operations, security forces and allied Tutsi militia have been accused of killings, house destruction, looting and rape.

"In January and February up to 122 people, including a 70-year-old man and six children are reported to have been killed in Rutegama commune. At the same time 272 people who had not regrouped, including an 81-year-old woman and a six-year-old child, were reportedly killed in Butaganzwa commune," it said.
Amnesty said in some cases whole families were slaughtered.

"In many cases house destruction, carried out by soldiers sometimes accompanied by members of Tutsi militias, appears to have taken place to make it impossible for the inhabitants to return to their homes," it said.
Amnesty said it had also received consistent reports of apparent disappearences of people. "Disappearances and extrajudicial executions may have routinely occurred," it said.
The group said hundreds were killed in the last few months in attacks on regroupment camps by unidentified people.
"In a war which is being played out largely on ethnic lines what effectively amounts to the isolation of ethnic groups into definable areas makes them vulnerable to attack," it added.
At least 150,000 people from both ethnic groups have been killed since 1993 in massacres and civil war since the assasination of the first freely elected president, Melchior Ndadaye, a Hutu.

Some political analysts fear unless brought under control, Burundi could go down the same path as equally ethnically-divided neighbouring Rwanda, where an estimated 800,000 people were slaughtered in three months of genocide in 1994.
